title: Decorator Pattern
oneLiner: Wraps an object to add new behavior at runtime, without touching the original class or spawning a subclass for every combination.

hero.name: Enhancer
hero.catchphrase: Wrap me. Stack me. Extend without altering.
hero.power: Layers new behavior onto an object at runtime by wrapping it, keeping every layer independently combinable.
hero.weakness: Stack enough decorators and it gets hard to tell which layer is responsible for which behavior — deep wrapping chains are hard to debug.
hero.origin: Enhancer showed up after a coffee-shop app shipped `DarkRoastWithMilkAndSugarAndWhip`, `DarkRoastWithMilk`, `LightRoastWithSugar` — a subclass for every single topping combination.

story.problem: A coffee-ordering app models every topping combination as its own subclass: `DarkRoastWithMilk`, `DarkRoastWithMilkAndSugar`, and so on. Every new topping doubles the subclass count.
story.solution: Enhancer wraps any `Beverage` in a `MilkDecorator`, `SugarDecorator`, or `WhipDecorator` — each one adds cost and description, then delegates the rest to whatever it's wrapping.
story.result: Any topping combination is just stacking decorators at order time. No new subclass is ever needed for a new combination.

before: Adding a topping multiplies the subclass count
Reusing topping logic across drinks means copy-paste
after: Adding a topping means one new decorator class
Any drink + any combination of toppings, no new class needed

panels.label: The Problem
panels.caption: A class list scrolls past: DarkRoastWithMilk, DarkRoastWithSugar, DarkRoastWithMilkAndSugar, DarkRoastWithMilkAndSugarAndWhip...
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: We added 'oat milk' as an option and just created twelve more subclasses. Twelve.

panels.label: The Hero Arrives
panels.caption: Enhancer appears, pulling on layer after layer of coats over a plain base.
panels.speaker: Enhancer
panels.dialogue: Stop subclassing every combination. Wrap the drink in toppings instead — stack as many layers as you want.

panels.label: Pattern Power
panels.caption: MilkDecorator wraps a Beverage. SugarDecorator wraps that. Each layer adds its own cost and description.
panels.speaker: Enhancer
panels.dialogue: new SugarDecorator(new MilkDecorator(new DarkRoast())). Each layer only knows its own job, then passes the rest down.

panels.label: The Result
panels.caption: The topping menu adds 'oat milk' as one new decorator class, combinable with everything already built.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: One new decorator, and it already works with every existing drink and every existing topping. No subclass explosion.

useWhen: You need to add behavior to individual objects at runtime, not to every instance of a class.
The number of possible feature combinations would otherwise require a subclass per combination.
You want to add and remove responsibilities dynamically, in any order, without touching the original class.
avoidWhen: There's only one or two fixed feature combinations — plain subclassing or a config flag is simpler.
The added behavior needs to know deep internals of the wrapped object (decorators should only interact through the public interface).
Deep decorator chains would make debugging ("which layer set this?") impractically hard for your team.
commonMistakes: Stacking so many decorators that stack traces and debugging become unreadable — nobody can tell which layer misbehaved.
Letting a decorator break the interface contract (e.g. changing a return type), so callers can't treat decorated and undecorated objects the same way.
Reaching for Decorator to add a single, permanent piece of behavior — a subclass or composition would be simpler and clearer.
Confusing Decorator (adds behavior, same interface) with Adapter (changes the interface) — they wrap, but for different reasons.
explanation.realWorldExample: Java's `BufferedReader(new FileReader(...))` and Node's stream `.pipe()` chains, Python decorators (a different but related idea), and UI component libraries wrapping components with `withLogging()`/`withAuth()` HOCs are all Decorator in spirit.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: This sounds like Composite — wrapping objects inside objects.

conversation.speaker: Enhancer
conversation.message: Related shape, different purpose. Composite is about treating trees and leaves the same. I'm about layering NEW BEHAVIOR onto one object, one wrap at a time.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: How many layers is too many?

conversation.speaker: Enhancer
conversation.message: When you can't explain what a stack of decorators does in one sentence, you've gone too deep. Keep each layer's job small and obvious.

codeBattle.scenario: Your logging library needs to support combinations of timestamping, log-level filtering, and JSON formatting, applied in any order, without a subclass for every combination.
codeBattle.question: Which hero should you call?
codeBattle.explanation: Enhancer lets each feature (timestamp, filter, format) be its own wrapper, stacked in any order without multiplying subclasses.

quiz.question: What does Decorator let you do that plain subclassing struggles with?
options: Add or remove behavior on individual objects at runtime, in any combination, without a subclass per combination
Guarantee an object has exactly one instance
Make two incompatible interfaces work together
Recursively treat a tree of objects and a single object identically
quiz.answer: Add or remove behavior on individual objects at runtime, in any combination, without a subclass per combination
quiz.explanation: Decorator trades subclass explosion for composable wrapper objects that layer behavior at runtime.

quiz.question: How does a Decorator typically implement the interface it shares with the object it wraps?
options: It adds its own behavior, then delegates the rest of the call to the wrapped object
It completely replaces the wrapped object's behavior
It ignores the wrapped object entirely
It converts the wrapped object into a different interface
quiz.answer: It adds its own behavior, then delegates the rest of the call to the wrapped object
quiz.explanation: The defining move is 'do my bit, then pass through' — that's what keeps decorators stackable.

quiz.question: What's a real risk of overusing Decorator?
options: Long decorator chains become hard to debug — it's unclear which layer is responsible for what
It always makes code run slower than inheritance, with no exceptions
It prevents objects from ever being garbage collected
It requires a database to track the wrapping order
quiz.answer: Long decorator chains become hard to debug — it's unclear which layer is responsible for what
quiz.explanation: Each added layer is another indirection to trace through when something goes wrong.

quiz.question: How does Decorator differ from Adapter?
options: Decorator keeps the same interface and adds behavior; Adapter changes the interface to make it compatible
They are the same pattern with different names
Adapter can only wrap one object; Decorator can wrap unlimited objects
Decorator requires inheritance; Adapter forbids it
quiz.answer: Decorator keeps the same interface and adds behavior; Adapter changes the interface to make it compatible
quiz.explanation: Both wrap an object, but for opposite reasons: Decorator preserves the interface while extending behavior, Adapter changes the interface to fix incompatibility.
